description: 3 pages, no headers or footers. Page 1: an 18pt centered title; two-column band A (216pt columns at x=72 and x=324, 10pt, 13pt leading) whose left column ends with the line "A-LEFT-END." and whose right column starts with "A-RIGHT-START."; a full-width 14pt centered pull-quote line starting "MID-FULL"; two-column band B whose columns start with "B-LEFT-START." and "B-RIGHT-START.". Page 2: one column; a 7pt chart axis line "0 10 20 30 40" at 70% of the page height with body paragraphs below it, then a real 7pt footnote near the bottom. Page 3: two columns starting at 480pt, each ending in its own 7pt footnote.
format: Per page: `lines` = expected buildLines(page).map(l => l.text) in reading order; `spoken` = text to speak with DEFAULT_FILTERS; `spokenReadEverything` = text to speak with READ_EVERYTHING; `skipped` = what DEFAULT_FILTERS drop. Spoken text joins lines with single spaces, de-hyphenates "-" + lowercase line starts, and is normalized (ligatures expanded, soft hyphens removed, NBSP/thin space -> space).
notes: The markers are ordinary words and are spoken.
The axis line "0 10 20 30 40" is spoken: it is not a footnote (no words) and not dropped by any other filter.
Page 3: both 7pt footnotes are dropped, one per column.

lines: Reading Order Around Full-Width Lines
Sleep research began with simple questions
about how long people rest each night. Early
laboratories recorded brain waves and found
regular cycles. Each cycle lasts about ninety
minutes.
A-LEFT-END.
A-RIGHT-START.
Memory benefits from those cycles in different
ways. Deep stages seem to strengthen facts,
while dreaming stages seem to link ideas
together. Students who sleep after studying
recall more the next morning.
MID-FULL a pulled quotation set across both columns of the page.
B-LEFT-START.
Napping has its own literature. A short nap of
twenty minutes improves alertness without
grogginess. Longer naps can leave a person
dazed for a while.
B-RIGHT-START.
Caffeine changes the picture. It blocks the signal
that builds up as the day goes on. The effect
fades after several hours.

lines: The survey asked students how many hours they slept before an exam. Most reported between six and
eight hours. A small group slept far less than that.
Scores rose with sleep up to eight hours and then levelled off. The gain was largest for students who had
slept five hours or less. The authors caution that the groups differed in other ways too.
Taken together, the results support a simple message about rest before an exam.
1 Percentages in this survey are rounded to whole numbers.

lines: Learning to read is a long process that begins
well before school. Children first notice that print
carries meaning. They then learn that letters
stand for sounds. Later they learn to blend those
sounds into words. Each step builds on the one
before it.
Parents can help by reading aloud every day.
Shared reading builds vocabulary and a love of
stories. Children who are read to often arrive at
school with a head start.
Teachers add structured practice with sounds
and spelling. Short daily lessons work better
than long weekly ones. Progress is checked
often, so that no child falls behind unnoticed.
1 Invented note on how the sample of children was chosen.
Reading for pleasure continues to matter in later
years. Teenagers who read for fun score higher
on tests of vocabulary. They also write more
fluently. The habit tends to fade in adolescence,
so schools try to protect it.
Libraries play a quiet part in this. A good library
offers choice, and choice is the surest way to
keep a reluctant reader turning pages. Many
libraries also run clubs that bring readers
together.
Finally, adults who read regularly report lower
stress. The effect appears after only a few
minutes a day, which is good news for busy
people.
2 Invented note on how the reading scores were scaled.
